docs.text: Open-source embedded C++ Write the driver once. Run it on any MCU. ¶ Kokeb Labs builds the software between your firmware and the chips on your board: C++20 drivers that never call a vendor SDK, a framework that joins them, and the tools and process that keep them trustworthy. You give a driver a few small functions for your bus, and the same code runs on ESP32, STM32, RP2040 or your laptop, where its tests run without hardware. MIT licensed. Browse the drivers Request a driver GitHub What Kokeb Labs is ¶ Kokeb (ኮከብ) means "star" in Amharic. Kokeb Labs is one project with four parts: Chip drivers One public repository per chip, named driver-<chip> : 22 today, from ADCs, encoders and sensors to motor controllers and a CANopen client. Each is a header-only C++20 library with a datasheet-backed documentation site. See the drivers Tooling and process driver-template starts a driver in one command, ci-tools gives every repository the same checks, docs and releases, and espidf-tools builds ESP-IDF apps. The handbook holds the rules the checks enforce. See the tooling Open boards KiCad boards built around the drivers, traced from needs to test results. A template, a parts library and a block library exist; the first board is at concept stage. See the boards A framework, coming kb-core joins drivers to ports and an RTOS layer, with ports for ESP32 and STM32. It is in development and not public yet. Drivers do not wait for it: they work on their own. Read the roadmap How the pieces fit ¶ How Kokeb Labs fits together Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your firmware calls the chip drivers directly today, or through kb-core when it is released; a driver reaches the chip only through the hooks of an MCU port, which is a short class you write or a ready one for ESP32 or STM32; the port drives the chip on your board. Dashed cards are in development or at an early stage. At the top right, the open boards your firmware can run on, built around the drivers. On the right, the tooling and process every repository uses: driver-template starts a driver, board-template starts a board, ci-tools checks, documents and releases them all, the handbook holds the rules the checks enforce, espidf-tools builds and flashes ESP-IDF projects, and driver-requests takes the requests for new drivers. Your firmware calls a driver. The driver knows the chip and nothing about your MCU: it reaches the bus only through the hooks of a port class. Beside that path sits the tooling lane: the templates start a repository, ci-tools runs the same checks in all of them, the handbook says what those checks enforce, and the request repository takes the asks for new drivers. Why it's different ¶ You write the port, not the driver A driver needs a few functions from you: bring the bus up, move bytes, wait. A C++20 concept checks them at compile time, so a missing or wrong hook is a compile error, not a crash on the bench. Tests before the board arrives Every driver builds and runs its tests on the host against a model of the chip written from the datasheet. A fuzzer corrupts the chip's replies, and compile-fail tests prove the port contract rejects what it should. Small and predictable Every call returns Result<T> with an error code. No exceptions, no heap, no RTTI, no virtual calls, so it fits small MCUs and safety reviews. Honest about status Each driver states how far it has been checked on real hardware as a level, H0 to H2. All 22 are at H0 today: host-tested and fuzzed, not yet verified on a bench. Every README says so. What a port looks like ¶ The whole MCU-specific part of an SPI driver, from driver-template . Fill in the bodies with your SDK's calls: #include "xmpl100.hpp" class MyPort : public xmpl100 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept ; // bring the bus up on the first call; true at once afterwards bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept ; // one transfer, CS held low void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept ; // wait at least us microseconds }; Then use the driver the same way on every board: xmpl100 :: XMPL100 < MyPort > sensor ( port ); // no I/O yet if ( auto r = sensor . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // bus up, reset, chip ID check return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus, Timeout or DeviceIdMismatch } const auto t = sensor . ReadTemperatureC (); // t.value in degrees Celsius, or t.error One measurement through a driver Figure description and sources The Firmware calls EnsureInitialized on the Driver. The Driver sends its first transfers to the Port, which moves the bytes on the bus to the Chip and returns the replies. The Driver checks the chip identity against the datasheet and returns a Result to the Firmware. A later measurement call goes through the Port the same way, and the Driver returns either the value in physical units or an Error, never a number it could not trust. Drawn from: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml . Built for firmware where a bug can hurt ¶ The process is written for software that may end up in a safety-classified product: MISRA C++:2023 checks on every pull request, an independent review of each driver, fuzzing, coverage gates, release candidates before releases and a stated hardware validation level. A Kokeb component is not a certified product; it supplies the evidence a manufacturer's own process asks for. Request a driver I want to write a driver Create a repository from the template and run one command. Your first build and tests pass before you change a line. docs.text: Contributing ¶ Good first contributions ¶ You can Where Fix a doc, a typo or a broken example Any repository; the docs live in docs/ Ask for a driver, or say which chip you need most Request a driver Add a vote to a request you also need A thumbs-up reaction on that request's issue Run a driver on a real chip and report what you saw The driver's repository; see hardware validation Report that a chip does not do what its datasheet says The datasheet erratum form Write a driver for a chip you know Start from driver-template and open a discussion first Ask for a port to an MCU family, SDK or RTOS The port request form Report a bug The repository's issues, with the bug form Issues labelled good first issue are a good start. Request a driver ¶ A driver is written only from public documents, so a request is a form with a link. Search the open and closed requests first; if the chip is already there, add a thumbs-up reaction. That is the vote. I want to Open A driver for a chip that has none Request a driver The drivers on an MCU family, SDK or RTOS without a port Request a port or target Report a datasheet erratum Datasheet erratum From a request to a release candidate Figure description and sources A request opens as Requested and becomes Triaged once a maintainer has found the part clear, not a duplicate and within scope. Datasheet acquired follows when the public documents cover the whole chip, then In design while the architecture note is written, Building while the driver, its tests and its docs are written, In review for the independent rounds and the local rehearsal of CI, and Released when a release candidate is out. A request that will not be done is Declined, with the reason in a comment. Drawn from: docs/model/request-pipeline.state.yml . Every request sits on the Driver pipeline board of the drivers organisation, and its Stage shows where it is. When you open or edit a request, a triage workflow reads your part number, labels the issue chip:<PART> , lists duplicates and existing drivers that may cover the part, and labels needs-datasheet or needs-info when something is missing. Editing the issue runs the check again. The datasheet link must be an https link on the chip vendor's own website , reachable without an account, and a link, never an attachment. Never link a document under NDA. The queue is ordered by votes, how complete the public documents are, effort (simpler chips go first) and help offered: someone who can test on hardware or review moves a request up. A request may be declined when the documents are not public, the part is obsolete, or it is a module whose firmware already hides the chip. The reason is always given in a comment. The request repository has every detail. How a change gets in ¶ Fork the repository and create a branch. Make the change, with its docs and tests in the same pull request. Sign off every commit: git commit -s . CI fails a pull request with a commit that has no matching Signed-off-by: line. Open the pull request. CI gate runs every check and tells you what is missing; a maintainer reviews. Workflows from a first-time contributor's fork wait for a maintainer's approval before they run. If a change affects behaviour on hardware, say in the pull request which MCU and board you ran it on and what you observed, or write "not verified on hardware" with the steps someone should run. Security ¶ Report a vulnerability privately through the repository's Security tab ("Report a vulnerability"), never in a public issue. The security policy says what happens next. Community ¶ Be kind and specific: the code of conduct applies everywhere. Full details are in the contributing guide . Questions and ideas go to Discussions ; anything else to kokeblabs@gmail.com .

docs.text: How we build ¶ A driver is the chip's datasheet turned into C++. We build each one as if it could end up in a safety-classified product, and we say plainly how far each one has got. The process in one picture ¶ What stands between a datasheet and a release candidate Figure description and sources The Inputs column holds the public datasheet and a model of the chip written from it, apart from the driver. The CI column holds host tests with compile-fail cases, sanitizers and fuzzing, coverage and complexity limits, clang-tidy and cppcheck, and the MISRA C++:2023 scan with the C++20 profile. The Review column holds an independent review round, where mutants of every fix must be caught by a test, and a check of every claim against the code. The Release column holds the release candidate, with its tag, its documentation site and its stated hardware level. Drawn from: docs/model/driver-gates.pipeline.yml . Practice What it means here Public datasheets only A driver is written from documents anyone can read. A chip whose register map is under NDA is declined IEC 62304, up to Class C The process maps onto the standard's clauses so a manufacturer can use a component in software of any safety class, Class C included. It is not a certificate: see below MISRA C++:2023 Every pull request runs the MISRA scan; each deviation is recorded with its reason Independent review A reviewer who did not write the driver, its model or its tests reviews it, in rounds, until nothing is left Fuzzing A fuzzer corrupts and replaces what the chip sends back and resets the chip at any point, on every pull request Mutation testing Reviewers break each fix on purpose; a test must fail on every mutant Coverage and complexity gates 85 % lines and 75 % branches at least, and limits on function size and complexity Release candidates Every driver ships as a -rc tag first, with its hardware level stated in the release text Hardware validation levels H0, H1 and H2 say how far the driver has been checked on a real chip A driver never touches the SDK ¶ Everything that depends on your MCU sits behind a small port class that you write, and the driver only calls its hooks. The driver owns Your port owns Register framing, reset and chip-ID checks, conversions, CRCs Bringing the bus up, moving bytes, optional GPIO, delay and log hooks Units, ranges and Config presets with datasheet defaults Pins, clocks, DMA, locking, which SPI or I2C peripheral The port derives from the driver's interface with CRTP ( class MyPort : public chip::SpiInterface<MyPort> ) and a C++20 concept checks every required hook at compile time. There are no virtual calls, so the compiler can inline the port into the driver. Predictable on small MCUs ¶ No exceptions, no heap, no RTTI. Every call returns Result<T> : a value, or an Error that says what went wrong ( Bus , Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , chip-specific faults). Nothing happens in a constructor. EnsureInitialized() does the first I/O, so you decide when the bus is touched. Bounded waits. A driver never blocks forever on a busy flag. No reading it can't trust. A driver reports a bad reading as an Error , not as a measurement: the BMP581 driver, for one, refuses a stuck line, a reset value and anything outside the measurement range. Brand-free ¶ A driver is named after its chip, not after a product: repository driver-<chip> , namespace <chip>:: . A product's pin map or modes never go into a shared repository. Kind of "specific" Example Where it lives Chip-specific the registers of one sensor that chip's driver MCU-specific an ESP-IDF SPI port a port, built only for that family Product-specific one product's pin map or modes the product's own repository, through extension points Tested without hardware ¶ Every driver builds and runs its tests on the host with CMake and ctest . The chip model is written from the datasheet, not from the driver, so a wrong constant in the driver can't hide behind the same wrong constant in the model. The model changes state on its own, resets mid-session and completes measurements in time, so a missed reset fails a test. Error paths are forced: every bus transfer fails in turn, and every error the driver can return is produced. Compile-fail tests check that a broken port does not compile. A fuzzer (libFuzzer with the address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers, 120 s per target on every pull request) corrupts the replies and checks that no broken line is returned as data. Every input that ever broke a promise stays in the replayed corpus, so a fixed bug stays fixed. One measurement through a driver Figure description and sources The Firmware calls EnsureInitialized on the Driver. The Driver sends its first transfers to the Port, which moves the bytes on the bus to the Chip and returns the replies. The Driver checks the chip identity against the datasheet and returns a Result to the Firmware. A later measurement call goes through the Port the same way, and the Driver returns either the value in physical units or an Error, never a number it could not trust. Drawn from: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml . Coding standards ¶ Standard Used for MISRA C++:2023 with Technical Corrigendum 1 (2026) C++ code. Every guideline is classified in a compliance matrix: decided by a tool, checked in review, left to a commercial checker, or not applicable with a reason MISRA C:2025 C code; its matrix follows the same format SEI CERT C++ and C Security baseline, checked by clang-tidy and cppcheck C++ Core Guidelines Design and idiom, through clang-tidy NASA/JPL Power of Ten Embedded discipline We follow the approach MISRA itself defines in MISRA Compliance:2020 : an enforcement plan, a re-categorisation plan where our profile is stricter, a deviation record for every departure from a required guideline, and a compliance summary with each release. Mandatory guidelines are never deviated. Every pull request runs the MISRA scan with the open CodeQL coding-standards pack on a host and a Cortex-M build; the commercial checker is added at the safety level . Independent review ¶ A review round is one independent reviewer, one fixer and one verdict, repeated until the stop rule holds. The reviewer did not write the driver, its model or its tests, works read-only, and never sees the builder's conclusions. Mechanical results come first: lint, the gate log and the CI lines are not re-argued. The reviewer verifies the previous round's fixes at the cause by building mutants : revert the fix, or change a constant in its guard. A fix is accepted only if a test fails on its mutant. Every claim in the docs and the build report ("never", "always", "returns") is checked against the code and a test. The judgement questions go to the reviewer: is the datasheet read correctly, is the state machine complete, is the model independent of the driver. Anything a script can decide moves out of review into lint or a test, so reviewers spend their time on judgement. Assurance levels ¶ Not every repository needs the same rigour. Each declares one of three levels, and each includes the one below it. What each assurance level asks for Figure description and sources Rows are the checks and evidence. Columns are the three assurance levels standard, high and safety. A cell says required, measured or not required in words and with a mark. Format, lint, static analysis, host tests, the strict documentation build, the sign-off check and the CI gate are required at every level. Sanitizers, a coverage floor, builds for every supported target, warning-free Doxygen on the public API and a deviation record for every suppressed finding start at high. Requirement traceability, full branch and MC/DC coverage, the coding-standard matrix with a commercial MISRA checker, an anomaly list and a signed evidence package start at safety. Drawn from: docs/model/assurance-levels.matrix.yml . Drivers are built at high from their first release. Safety is chosen per component, when a product team intends to qualify it, and commits the project to keeping the evidence current for every release. Using a component in a medical device ¶ IEC 62304 applies to a manufacturer's process, not to a library. A manufacturer can use a Kokeb component as SOUP (software of unknown provenance), or bring it under their own process by forking it at a release. The handbook's IEC 62304 page maps each clause of the standard onto what a component provides. A component at the safety level is not "IEC 62304 compliant": risk management, hazard analysis, system testing and the device's technical file stay with the manufacturer. Releases and release candidates ¶ The driver is built and reviewed until the full local rehearsal of CI passes. It is published in a public repository, and main must be green with its docs published. The first tag is a release candidate, vX.Y.Z-rc.1 . Its release text states the hardware level. A release candidate publishes its docs under its own tag and does not move latest . A release candidate that passes the bench is tagged again, on the same commit, as vX.Y.Z . All 22 public drivers are at v0.1.0-rc.1 today. Hardware validation levels ¶ Tests prove the driver against a model of the chip written from the datasheet. A bench proves the model. Each driver states how far it has been checked as a level, in its metadata and as a badge on its README. Hardware validation levels Figure description and sources A driver starts at H0, where it has only been run against a model of the chip on the host. It reaches H1 when a defined bench rig has run the example and the rig document and the logs are kept. It reaches H2 when a hardware engineer has reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off. The level is written in the driver's metadata file and shown as a badge on its README. Drawn from: docs/model/hardware-levels.state.yml . Level Means H0 Host model only: never run on a chip. Releases say not hardware-verified H1 A defined bench rig ran the example; the rig document and the logs are kept H2 A hardware engineer reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off Every public driver is at H0 today. We don't call a driver verified without the evidence for H1 or H2. Language standard ¶ Drivers target C++20 today. One language level across every repository lets any driver sit under any library. C++20 gives concepts for the port contract, requires for optional hooks, std::span for caller buffers and designated initialisers for configuration, and it is supported by ESP-IDF 5.x and current STM32 toolchains without the lag that C++23 has on vendor compilers. It is checked, not assumed. Every target builds as ISO C++20 with compiler extensions off and -pedantic-errors , and every public header also compiles on its own at -std=c++20 with each compiler the repository ships for. ESP-IDF's own default dialect is newer, so without that check a C++23 feature would compile on one toolchain and break on another. It is a profile, not "anything in C++20". MISRA C++:2023 is written for C++17, so the handbook's C++20 profile sorts the features into use, use with rules and forbid: 58 guidelines (4 mandatory, 36 required, 18 advisory). Anything from C++23 or later is a violation even where the compiler accepts it. It is recorded. A driver states its standard in its README badge and its build settings ( cxx_std_20 ). Raising the compiler a caller needs is a breaking change, so a release that does it lists it under Breaking in its changelog. It will move up. There is no date, and a move is not a surprise. It happens when all of these hold: Condition Why Every compiler we ship for supports the standard: the ESP-IDF toolchain, the CI compilers and the Cortex-M toolchain A language level that one target can't build is not a level The C++20 profile and its MISRA mapping are extended to it, in one pull request with the rule list and the deviation record The coding standard fixes the language standard, so the checks must know the new one first A decision record replaces ADR-0010 A rule is not loosened or changed without a recorded reason The release that adopts it lists the new compiler requirement as breaking Callers choose when to move The same checks in every repository ¶ Check What it catches Strict docs build, link check, figure and generated-table drift Broken links, stale diagrams, docs that disagree with the code Host build and tests, clang-tidy, cppcheck Bugs, undefined behaviour, the port contract clang-format, markdownlint, yamllint Style drift DCO sign-off, required files, MIT licence Provenance and licensing The handbook check Rules with an ID, run as code CI gate One required check that passes only when everything else did The rules are in the handbook . Every rule has an ID, a level and the check that verifies it. Supply-chain hygiene ¶ Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA on a real release tag and reviewed before it is allowed in the organisation; tools without a trusted action are downloaded from their own release and checked against a pinned SHA-256. Dependabot keeps the pins current. Secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot alerts and CodeQL are on for every repository. Licence and sign-off ¶ Everything is MIT licensed, Copyright (c) 2026 The Kokeb Labs Authors . There is no CLA: you sign off each commit ( git commit -s ) to certify the Developer Certificate of Origin .

docs.text: What stands between a datasheet and a release candidate Figure description and sources The Inputs column holds the public datasheet and a model of the chip written from it, apart from the driver. The CI column holds host tests with compile-fail cases, sanitizers and fuzzing, coverage and complexity limits, clang-tidy and cppcheck, and the MISRA C++:2023 scan with the C++20 profile. The Review column holds an independent review round, where mutants of every fix must be caught by a test, and a check of every claim against the code. The Release column holds the release candidate, with its tag, its documentation site and its stated hardware level. Drawn from: docs/model/driver-gates.pipeline.yml . Practice What it means here Public datasheets only A driver is written from documents anyone can read. A chip whose register map is under NDA is declined IEC 62304, up to Class C The process maps onto the standard's clauses so a manufacturer can use a component in software of any safety class, Class C included. It is not a certificate: see below MISRA C++:2023 Every pull request runs the MISRA scan; each deviation is recorded with its reason Independent review A reviewer who did not write the driver, its model or its tests reviews it, in rounds, until nothing is left Fuzzing A fuzzer corrupts and replaces what the chip sends back and resets the chip at any point, on every pull request Mutation testing Reviewers break each fix on purpose; a test must fail on every mutant Coverage and complexity gates 85 % lines and 75 % branches at least, and limits on function size and complexity Release candidates Every driver ships as a -rc tag first, with its hardware level stated in the release text Hardware validation levels H0, H1 and H2 say how far the driver has been checked on a real chip
docs.title: The process in one picture

docs.text: Everything that depends on your MCU sits behind a small port class that you write, and the driver only calls its hooks. The driver owns Your port owns Register framing, reset and chip-ID checks, conversions, CRCs Bringing the bus up, moving bytes, optional GPIO, delay and log hooks Units, ranges and Config presets with datasheet defaults Pins, clocks, DMA, locking, which SPI or I2C peripheral The port derives from the driver's interface with CRTP ( class MyPort : public chip::SpiInterface<MyPort> ) and a C++20 concept checks every required hook at compile time. There are no virtual calls, so the compiler can inline the port into the driver.
docs.title: A driver never touches the SDK

docs.text: No exceptions, no heap, no RTTI. Every call returns Result<T> : a value, or an Error that says what went wrong ( Bus , Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , chip-specific faults). Nothing happens in a constructor. EnsureInitialized() does the first I/O, so you decide when the bus is touched. Bounded waits. A driver never blocks forever on a busy flag. No reading it can't trust. A driver reports a bad reading as an Error , not as a measurement: the BMP581 driver, for one, refuses a stuck line, a reset value and anything outside the measurement range.
docs.title: Predictable on small MCUs

docs.text: A driver is named after its chip, not after a product: repository driver-<chip> , namespace <chip>:: . A product's pin map or modes never go into a shared repository. Kind of "specific" Example Where it lives Chip-specific the registers of one sensor that chip's driver MCU-specific an ESP-IDF SPI port a port, built only for that family Product-specific one product's pin map or modes the product's own repository, through extension points
docs.title: Brand-free

docs.text: Every driver builds and runs its tests on the host with CMake and ctest . The chip model is written from the datasheet, not from the driver, so a wrong constant in the driver can't hide behind the same wrong constant in the model. The model changes state on its own, resets mid-session and completes measurements in time, so a missed reset fails a test. Error paths are forced: every bus transfer fails in turn, and every error the driver can return is produced. Compile-fail tests check that a broken port does not compile. A fuzzer (libFuzzer with the address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers, 120 s per target on every pull request) corrupts the replies and checks that no broken line is returned as data. Every input that ever broke a promise stays in the replayed corpus, so a fixed bug stays fixed. One measurement through a driver Figure description and sources The Firmware calls EnsureInitialized on the Driver. The Driver sends its first transfers to the Port, which moves the bytes on the bus to the Chip and returns the replies. The Driver checks the chip identity against the datasheet and returns a Result to the Firmware. A later measurement call goes through the Port the same way, and the Driver returns either the value in physical units or an Error, never a number it could not trust. Drawn from: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml .
docs.title: Tested without hardware

docs.text: Standard Used for MISRA C++:2023 with Technical Corrigendum 1 (2026) C++ code. Every guideline is classified in a compliance matrix: decided by a tool, checked in review, left to a commercial checker, or not applicable with a reason MISRA C:2025 C code; its matrix follows the same format SEI CERT C++ and C Security baseline, checked by clang-tidy and cppcheck C++ Core Guidelines Design and idiom, through clang-tidy NASA/JPL Power of Ten Embedded discipline We follow the approach MISRA itself defines in MISRA Compliance:2020 : an enforcement plan, a re-categorisation plan where our profile is stricter, a deviation record for every departure from a required guideline, and a compliance summary with each release. Mandatory guidelines are never deviated. Every pull request runs the MISRA scan with the open CodeQL coding-standards pack on a host and a Cortex-M build; the commercial checker is added at the safety level .
docs.title: Coding standards

docs.text: A review round is one independent reviewer, one fixer and one verdict, repeated until the stop rule holds. The reviewer did not write the driver, its model or its tests, works read-only, and never sees the builder's conclusions. Mechanical results come first: lint, the gate log and the CI lines are not re-argued. The reviewer verifies the previous round's fixes at the cause by building mutants : revert the fix, or change a constant in its guard. A fix is accepted only if a test fails on its mutant. Every claim in the docs and the build report ("never", "always", "returns") is checked against the code and a test. The judgement questions go to the reviewer: is the datasheet read correctly, is the state machine complete, is the model independent of the driver. Anything a script can decide moves out of review into lint or a test, so reviewers spend their time on judgement.
docs.title: Independent review

docs.text: Not every repository needs the same rigour. Each declares one of three levels, and each includes the one below it. What each assurance level asks for Figure description and sources Rows are the checks and evidence. Columns are the three assurance levels standard, high and safety. A cell says required, measured or not required in words and with a mark. Format, lint, static analysis, host tests, the strict documentation build, the sign-off check and the CI gate are required at every level. Sanitizers, a coverage floor, builds for every supported target, warning-free Doxygen on the public API and a deviation record for every suppressed finding start at high. Requirement traceability, full branch and MC/DC coverage, the coding-standard matrix with a commercial MISRA checker, an anomaly list and a signed evidence package start at safety. Drawn from: docs/model/assurance-levels.matrix.yml . Drivers are built at high from their first release. Safety is chosen per component, when a product team intends to qualify it, and commits the project to keeping the evidence current for every release.
docs.title: Assurance levels

docs.text: IEC 62304 applies to a manufacturer's process, not to a library. A manufacturer can use a Kokeb component as SOUP (software of unknown provenance), or bring it under their own process by forking it at a release. The handbook's IEC 62304 page maps each clause of the standard onto what a component provides. A component at the safety level is not "IEC 62304 compliant": risk management, hazard analysis, system testing and the device's technical file stay with the manufacturer.
docs.title: Using a component in a medical device

docs.text: The driver is built and reviewed until the full local rehearsal of CI passes. It is published in a public repository, and main must be green with its docs published. The first tag is a release candidate, vX.Y.Z-rc.1 . Its release text states the hardware level. A release candidate publishes its docs under its own tag and does not move latest . A release candidate that passes the bench is tagged again, on the same commit, as vX.Y.Z . All 22 public drivers are at v0.1.0-rc.1 today.
docs.title: Releases and release candidates

docs.text: Tests prove the driver against a model of the chip written from the datasheet. A bench proves the model. Each driver states how far it has been checked as a level, in its metadata and as a badge on its README. Hardware validation levels Figure description and sources A driver starts at H0, where it has only been run against a model of the chip on the host. It reaches H1 when a defined bench rig has run the example and the rig document and the logs are kept. It reaches H2 when a hardware engineer has reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off. The level is written in the driver's metadata file and shown as a badge on its README. Drawn from: docs/model/hardware-levels.state.yml . Level Means H0 Host model only: never run on a chip. Releases say not hardware-verified H1 A defined bench rig ran the example; the rig document and the logs are kept H2 A hardware engineer reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off Every public driver is at H0 today. We don't call a driver verified without the evidence for H1 or H2.
docs.title: Hardware validation levels

docs.text: Drivers target C++20 today. One language level across every repository lets any driver sit under any library. C++20 gives concepts for the port contract, requires for optional hooks, std::span for caller buffers and designated initialisers for configuration, and it is supported by ESP-IDF 5.x and current STM32 toolchains without the lag that C++23 has on vendor compilers. It is checked, not assumed. Every target builds as ISO C++20 with compiler extensions off and -pedantic-errors , and every public header also compiles on its own at -std=c++20 with each compiler the repository ships for. ESP-IDF's own default dialect is newer, so without that check a C++23 feature would compile on one toolchain and break on another. It is a profile, not "anything in C++20". MISRA C++:2023 is written for C++17, so the handbook's C++20 profile sorts the features into use, use with rules and forbid: 58 guidelines (4 mandatory, 36 required, 18 advisory). Anything from C++23 or later is a violation even where the compiler accepts it. It is recorded. A driver states its standard in its README badge and its build settings ( cxx_std_20 ). Raising the compiler a caller needs is a breaking change, so a release that does it lists it under Breaking in its changelog. It will move up. There is no date, and a move is not a surprise. It happens when all of these hold: Condition Why Every compiler we ship for supports the standard: the ESP-IDF toolchain, the CI compilers and the Cortex-M toolchain A language level that one target can't build is not a level The C++20 profile and its MISRA mapping are extended to it, in one pull request with the rule list and the deviation record The coding standard fixes the language standard, so the checks must know the new one first A decision record replaces ADR-0010 A rule is not loosened or changed without a recorded reason The release that adopts it lists the new compiler requirement as breaking Callers choose when to move
docs.title: Language standard

docs.text: Check What it catches Strict docs build, link check, figure and generated-table drift Broken links, stale diagrams, docs that disagree with the code Host build and tests, clang-tidy, cppcheck Bugs, undefined behaviour, the port contract clang-format, markdownlint, yamllint Style drift DCO sign-off, required files, MIT licence Provenance and licensing The handbook check Rules with an ID, run as code CI gate One required check that passes only when everything else did The rules are in the handbook . Every rule has an ID, a level and the check that verifies it.
docs.title: The same checks in every repository

docs.text: Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA on a real release tag and reviewed before it is allowed in the organisation; tools without a trusted action are downloaded from their own release and checked against a pinned SHA-256. Dependabot keeps the pins current. Secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot alerts and CodeQL are on for every repository.
docs.title: Supply-chain hygiene

Create a repository from the template, run python3 tools/setup.py , answer a few questions (chip name, bus, description), and you get: A C++20 driver skeleton for an SPI, I2C or UART chip, or a header-only library, with the port contract checked by a concept at compile time. Repository Using the template ci-tools v1 ¶ The CI and documentation platform every repository uses. Short caller workflows pin @v1 and get fixes without breaking changes. C++ build and host tests, clang-format, clang-tidy and cppcheck over one compile database. The MISRA C++:2023 scan, mutation testing, ESP-IDF firmware builds across versions with a size report, and releases that ship the exact firmware CI built. Every third-party action pinned to a commit SHA and reviewed before it is allowed. Documentation Repository handbook Ready ¶ Every rule for C, C++, CMake, tests, docs, Git, CI and coding agents, with the check that verifies it. A rule has an ID, a level and a named way of being checked. The handbook also holds the C++20 profile, the MISRA C++:2023 compliance matrix, the assurance levels and the page on using a component under IEC 62304. Handbook Repository espidf-tools v1 ¶ Build, flash and monitor every app of a multi-app ESP-IDF project. List the apps, ESP-IDF versions, build types and target once in app_config.yml ; the same scripts run on your machine and in CI. build_app.sh and flash_app.sh for any app, build type and ESP-IDF version, each built into its own folder. manage_idf.sh installs and switches ESP-IDF versions; serial-port detection, logs and tab completion included. generate_matrix.py turns app_config.yml into a CI matrix, so CI builds exactly what you build locally. Documentation Repository .github ¶ The organisation's profile, community files (contributing, code of conduct, security policy), the brand, the engineering standard and the settings of every repository kept as code. Repository Open boards ¶ Boards are built around the drivers and traced from what people need down to the part and its test results. All of them are early: nothing has been manufactured or verified on hardware yet. board-template Version 0 ¶ Start a new board in one command. Create a repository from the template, run python3 tools/setup.py , and you get: A board record ( board.yml ) with the status, the revision, the intended use and the drivers the board is built around. A requirements trace: needs, requirements, risks and verifications as data, linked by the version of what they derive from, so a change to a need or a chip flags everything that depends on it. A check that fails CI on broken or suspect links, unverified requirements and missing evidence, with its tests. Folders and rules for the KiCad project, the enclosure, the firmware, the manufacturing package and the test results, and the outline of the evidence pack a release carries. Repository The boards organisation Concept ¶ Repository What it is Status board-bmp581-breakout The first board: a breakout for the Bosch BMP581 pressure sensor, built around driver-bmp581 Concept: nothing built or verified kokeb-libs KiCad symbols, footprints and 3D models, each with a review status and a datasheet reference Concept: record format and checker exist, no library files yet kokeb-blocks Reusable circuit blocks (power, interfaces, sensor front ends) that boards are assembled from Concept: record format and checker exist, no blocks yet In development Not public yet ¶ kb-core , the framework: interface concepts, handlers that join drivers to them, small RTOS wrappers and utilities, with chip drivers pinned as release tags. Pick your MCU, RTOS and drivers in one CMake file; only what you pick is built. MCU ports for ESP32 and STM32: ready-made implementations of the bus, GPIO, timer and RTOS interfaces that drivers and handlers bind to. These repositories are private while they are in development. Drivers do not depend on them: a driver works with a port class you write yourself, and that stays true. See the roadmap .

docs.text: Roadmap ¶ This is where things stand, in order. We don't publish dates: a step moves to done when its evidence exists. Foundations Done The organisation and its settings as code, ci-tools v1, espidf-tools v1, driver-template , the handbook and the documentation platform, and this portal. Chip drivers 22 release candidates 22 public drivers, each tagged v0.1.0-rc.1 with host tests, a fuzzer, MISRA C++:2023 checks, an ESP32 example and a documentation site, in the kokeb-labs-drivers organisation. The driver request pipeline decides which chip comes next. Hardware validation Next Every driver is at level H0 today. A driver moves to H1 when a defined bench rig has run its example with the logs kept, and to H2 when a hardware engineer signs off. A release candidate that passes the bench is tagged again, on the same commit, as its release. Help with a bench is welcome: see contributing . kb-core and MCU ports In development The framework that joins drivers to interfaces, handlers and an RTOS layer, and ports for ESP32 and STM32. These repositories are not public yet. Drivers stay usable without them. docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs kokeb-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. What each assurance level asks for ¶ What each assurance level asks for Figure description and sources Rows are the checks and evidence. Columns are the three assurance levels standard, high and safety. A cell says required, measured or not required in words and with a mark. Format, lint, static analysis, host tests, the strict documentation build, the sign-off check and the CI gate are required at every level. Sanitizers, a coverage floor, builds for every supported target, warning-free Doxygen on the public API and a deviation record for every suppressed finding start at high. Requirement traceability, full branch and MC/DC coverage, the coding-standard matrix with a commercial MISRA checker, an anomaly list and a signed evidence package start at safety. Drawn from: docs/model/assurance-levels.matrix.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/assurance-levels.matrix.yml Drawn from: docs/model/assurance-levels.matrix.yml What stands between a datasheet and a release candidate ¶ What stands between a datasheet and a release candidate Figure description and sources The Inputs column holds the public datasheet and a model of the chip written from it, apart from the driver. The CI column holds host tests with compile-fail cases, sanitizers and fuzzing, coverage and complexity limits, clang-tidy and cppcheck, and the MISRA C++:2023 scan with the C++20 profile. The Review column holds an independent review round, where mutants of every fix must be caught by a test, and a check of every claim against the code. The Release column holds the release candidate, with its tag, its documentation site and its stated hardware level. Drawn from: docs/model/driver-gates.pipeline.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/driver-gates.pipeline.yml Drawn from: docs/model/driver-gates.pipeline.yml Hardware validation levels ¶ Hardware validation levels Figure description and sources A driver starts at H0, where it has only been run against a model of the chip on the host. It reaches H1 when a defined bench rig has run the example and the rig document and the logs are kept. It reaches H2 when a hardware engineer has reviewed the rig and the steps and signed off. The level is written in the driver's metadata file and shown as a badge on its README. Drawn from: docs/model/hardware-levels.state.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/hardware-levels.state.yml Drawn from: docs/model/hardware-levels.state.yml One measurement through a driver ¶ One measurement through a driver Figure description and sources The Firmware calls EnsureInitialized on the Driver. The Driver sends its first transfers to the Port, which moves the bytes on the bus to the Chip and returns the replies. The Driver checks the chip identity against the datasheet and returns a Result to the Firmware. A later measurement call goes through the Port the same way, and the Driver returns either the value in physical units or an Error, never a number it could not trust. Drawn from: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/one-measurement.seq.yml From a request to a release candidate ¶ From a request to a release candidate Figure description and sources A request opens as Requested and becomes Triaged once a maintainer has found the part clear, not a duplicate and within scope. Datasheet acquired follows when the public documents cover the whole chip, then In design while the architecture note is written, Building while the driver, its tests and its docs are written, In review for the independent rounds and the local rehearsal of CI, and Released when a release candidate is out. A request that will not be done is Declined, with the reason in a comment. Drawn from: docs/model/request-pipeline.state.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/request-pipeline.state.yml Drawn from: docs/model/request-pipeline.state.yml How Kokeb Labs fits together ¶ How Kokeb Labs fits together Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your firmware calls the chip drivers directly today, or through kb-core when it is released; a driver reaches the chip only through the hooks of an MCU port, which is a short class you write or a ready one for ESP32 or STM32; the port drives the chip on your board. Dashed cards are in development or at an early stage. At the top right, the open boards your firmware can run on, built around the drivers. On the right, the tooling and process every repository uses: driver-template starts a driver, board-template starts a board, ci-tools checks, documents and releases them all, the handbook holds the rules the checks enforce, espidf-tools builds and flashes ESP-IDF projects, and driver-requests takes the requests for new drivers. Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/system-map.py
